title: I let Siri listen to my conversations for weeks. Here’s what it got right — and very wrong | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

I found something surprising when I opened my iPhone’s Siri app last weekend: a summary of a private conversation with my husband.

The summary itself wasn’t the surprising part; I turned on a new Apple Watch feature that, with my permission, passively takes notes on conversations. What shocked me, however, was that it was wrong about a key health-related detail in our chat.

The new feature, called Siri Recap, can monitor conversations and generate high-level summaries. The idea is to have Siri be like a personal assistant that can jot down details you may have forgotten during a meeting, lecture or conversation, like an action item or TV show recommendation from a friend.

It’s part of Apple’s push to make its products more personal and helpful with artificial intelligence, an ambition that got off to a rocky start after Sirifaced multiple delays. The iPhone maker is racing against other tech giants to create sophisticated AI assistants that can better understand users’ daily lives, both online and off.

But Apple is looking to avoid the privacy concernsraised by its rivals. Siri Recap doesn’t record or save audio, nor does it identify speakers or produce a full transcript.

However, because it has less information on users, the Siri Recap summaries aren’t as useful compared to other AI tools.And some experts still take issue with the feature, saying capturing audio at all – even if it isn’t stored – is worrisome.

Siri Recap is currently in beta, which means Apple is still updating and improving it, and the company has not yet said when it will launch more broadly. It’s compatible with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, which must be paired with an iPhone 16 or later, not including the iPhone 16e.

The idea of Siri listening in on conversations would surely raise privacy concerns. So, Apple created a system that it claims can prevent anyone, including itself, from obtaining audio captured by the watch.

The Apple Watch captures audio in a secure section of the smartwatch’s processor that’s kept separate from other computing operations. The audio is then shared with the iPhone, which keeps this data separate, and translated into a condensed text version. That shortened version is then sent to Apple’s cloud computing platform where it’s summarized.

The audio is discarded before it leaves a user’s phone and is never saved, Apple says.

Beyond how the data is handled, Apple keeps its recaps intentionally vague. Unlike other AI wearables, Siri doesn’t provide a full transcript, and most of the time it omits specific names and details.

That has its pros and cons. It feels much less intrusive thanother AI gadgetsI’ve tested, like the Amazon Bee bracelet and Plaud NotePin S, both to myself and the people around me.

Butthere’s also less transparency. Smart glasses and recording accessories light up to indicate when they’re recording, though those lights aren’t always easy to see.The Apple Watch, on the other hand, doesn’t have a visual indicator when it’s activated because it’s not actually recording.

It can also be harder to explain Siri Recap. When I record interviews at work or use a device like Bee, I usually ask the people I’m with for consent. But Siri Recap is more challenging to describe since it’s not producing a recording or transcript. And since it’s on until I turn it off, I’ve accidentally captured private conversations I didn’t want summarized.

The proliferation of wearable gadgets that can record or document conversations – like watches, glasses and pins – could create broader unease in public, experts say.

“That’s going to change interactions, if everybody’s worried about somebody wearing a wire at all times,” said Irina Raicu, director of the internet ethics program at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics.

As for the question of whether these recaps are actually useful: They’re sort of like AI-generated summaries but for real life instead of news articles or phone notifications. You can get the gist of the conversation, but it’s not always going to highlight the information you’re looking for, and sometimes it’s inaccurate.

The summaries, which range in length depending on the conversation, were helpful at times. One recap of a chat with a colleague included a detail I wanted to include in an upcoming story that I may have otherwise forgotten.

Another summarymentioned a musical artist I recommended to a friend during karaoke, reminding me to text them about it. And when I showed a meeting recap to a coworker who couldn’t attend, she said the overview gave her a good gist of what she had missed.

The problem, though, is that it’s hard to extract much value from these summaries on most occasions. Keeping things vague preserves privacy, but it also makes the recaps far less informative and often too vague to be useful.

One log titled “Thanksgiving Week Work and Family Plans,” for example, has a bullet point that just says: “Reassurance given that there will be enough food.”

There are also concerns about whether the information Apple chooses to omit could unintentionally alter the meaning of a summarized conversation.

“So much of the meaning of conversations comes in those suggestions and tones, and you know whatever they deem non-essential language,” said Raicu.

The summaries also aren’t always accurate. One recap said I was at music trivia when I was actually at a karaoke party. Another time, it misunderstood a story a friend told me about an acquaintance whowas helping produce a musical in Los Angeles. Siri thought I was the one producing the show.

Other times, Siri recapped dialogue from a TV show or video game – which could be useful. But it was presented the same way as a real conversation in the Siri app, which can be confusing.

Siri Recap’s limitations may not matter right now; it only works on certain Apple Watches and iPhones, and people can simply choose not to use it at all. But it speaks to the broader challenge Apple faces in the AI race: How do you make a personal assistant that knows more about you while still preserving privacy?

It may be impossible to do both, according to Calli Schroeder,director of the AI and human rights program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center.

“Consider the bigger impact on society when suddenly you have to be concerned that anywhere you go, any conversation you have, any interaction with a friend or loved one, could be being processed through this technology,” she said.
